newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week-FOMC takes eyes off UK election.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week-FOMC takes eyes off UK election.

text.p: UK gilts will suffer more flutters over fears of a U.S. interest rate rise this week than from political sideswipes as the UK election campaign cools off for the Easter break on Friday.

HSBC Markets analyst Don Smith said "everything paled into insignificance" beside the meeting of the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on Tuesday, as dealers fear a 1/4 point rate hike may be announced.
Smith said the market had factored in a tightening, but he thought Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan would wait another month before raising rates.

"Gilts would get some support from a decision not to raise rates," said Smith. "If, on the other hand, Greenspan does increase by a 1/4 percent, that will undoubtedly send the market off - but only slightly as the market's looking further ahead."
U.S. central bank policymakers were expected to vote to tighten rates in order to cool rapid growth, which analysts say could reach four percent in the first quarter of 1997.

"A rate rise in the U.S. would be negative for global bond markets and would confirm we are heading for a change in the interest rate cycle this year," Graham McDevitt, head of bond strategy at Paribas Capital Markets in London said.
Analysts said the success of Wednesday's 10-year gilt auction would hinge on the FOMC meeting, although the market had been making room for the new benchmark issue for some time.

"Volume is going to stay very thin on Monday and Tuesday," said Kleinwort Benson analyst Steve Scott, "But buying at the auction may be a natural way back into the market. There's a good chance of prices going up after the auction."
The Bank of England is to issue 2.5 billion sterling worth of debt with a 2007 maturity and 7.25 percent yield.
Gilts were unmoved by Monday's revised fourth quarter GDP data as it barely changed provisional estimates.
Final quarter growth was unchanged at 0.8 percent, while the year-on-year figure was revised down to 2.6 percent from 2.7.

Also released were balance of payment figures showing that the current account was virtually in balance in 1996, its best performance since a small surplus in 1985. Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said they showed the UK economy was not out of control and that "the boom was not a consumer bubble".
On the political front, the last thing the gilt market wants is a revival of support for the ruling Conservative Party, currently 20 points and more behind in the polls.

UK markets have always favoured the Tories but far more of a problem than a Labour government, which has shed its tax and spending image, would be the uncertainty of a hung parliament or coalition government.
Gilts showed signs of volatility last week after Prime Minister John Major set Britain's election date for May 1, but traders said they expected the initial rumbles to settle down.
"We're in for a quiet couple of weeks on the political front," said Smith, "It's a long election campaign. The parties aren't going to fire all their ammunition straight away."
Analysts said a perceived revival in Conservative party support could widen gilt/bund yield spread.
Gilts were trading 185 basis points over 10-year Bunds on Monday. Just before the 1992 election that spread ballooned to 227 as fears of a Labour government gripped the market.

This time, Labour is a very different prospect. Merrill Lynch economists said a Labour lead was narrowing the yield spread as investors weighed up the relative prospects of Britain's joining a European single currency under a Labour government, and the possibility of a tougher monetary stance.
UK trade data due Wednesday at 0930 GMT is expected to show Britain's trade gap with non-European nations has narrowed, according to a Reuter poll of economists.

January figures for trade with non-European nations, released last month, showed Britain's trade shortfall dropped to 398 million stg from 640 million the month before. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
